title: Quantum neuroplastic learning for time-series processing
abstract: Quantum machine learning uses quantum states and dynamics to represent and process data. In quantum reservoir computing, the physical system is typically fixed and a classical readout is trained. Inspired by the formation, strengthening and pruning of synapses during biological learning, we propose quantum neuroplastic learning (QNL), which reorganizes the couplings among the qubits of a quantum reservoir, much as experience rewires connections among neurons. Eligibility traces guide local edits to couplings, fields, gate angles and evolution time, and an edit is retained when a statistical bound on its improvement exceeds a complexity cost. We evaluate QNL under restarting and online monitored protocols on short- and long-term memory, nonlinear autoregressive processing and forecasting, and channel equalization tasks. In simulation, QNL enhances memory capacity, develops long-term recall and sustains adaptation across multiple tasks, with the largest benefit for tasks that require extended memory. On the IBM superconducting processor \texttt{ibm\_fez}, with six seven-qubit reservoirs running in parallel on 42 qubits (1.28 million shots in total), configurations learned in simulation and frozen before execution reduced the channel-equalization symbol error rate from 9.7\% to 2.2\% and achieved a lower error rate than a matched-budget tuned baseline.
summary: This paper introduces Quantum Neuroplastic Learning (QNL), a method that allows the physical structure of a quantum reservoir to adapt its couplings during training, mimicking biological synaptic plasticity. By implementing this structural learning, QNL significantly boosts the memory capacity and performance of quantum machine learning models. The results demonstrate superior error rate reductions on superconducting quantum hardware compared to fixed-parameter approaches.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need for a learning principle in quantum reservoir computing (QRC) that allows the physical structure of the quantum reservoir to adapt dynamically, mimicking biological neuroplasticity.
main_result: Quantum Neuroplastic Learning (QNL) significantly enhances the memory capacity and long-term recall of the reservoir, achieving substantial error rate reductions (e.g., 9.7% to 2.2% in channel equalization) on real quantum hardware compared to fixed configurations.
method: QNL proposes reorganizing the reservoir couplings ($	heta$) using local, discrete edits guided by eligibility traces, admitting an edit only if its predicted loss reduction exceeds a complexity cost.
model_or_system: The system is a quantum reservoir computer, modeled using superconducting qubits (e.g., on the ibm fez processor) governed by various Hamiltonians (e.g., transverse-field Ising or circuit ansatz). The process involves training the reservoir structure ($	heta$) alongside the classical readout weights ($w$).
key_observables: Memory capacity ($C_	au$), symbol error rate (SER) for channel equalization, and Test Root-Mean-Square Error (RMSE) for time-series forecasting.
important_parameters: Complexity cost ($\alpha$), measurement budget ($N_{shots}$), Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR), and the specific quantum hardware platform (ibm fez).
main_assumptions: The readout weights ($w$) are refitted for every evaluated configuration, and the cost is paid in additional evaluations during the learning process.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the biological analogy of plasticity (synaptic tags) and its mapping to the physical configuration updates ($	heta$) in QNL. Other figures compare capacity and error rates across different learning protocols and hardware platforms.
paper_structure: The paper introduces QNL as a structural plasticity mechanism for QRC, details the update rules using eligibility traces, and then evaluates this method across multiple tasks (memory, forecasting, equalization) using both simulation and actual superconducting quantum hardware.
why_interesting: The integration of structural plasticity concepts, borrowed from neuroscience, into quantum machine learning models provides a powerful, biologically inspired mechanism for improving quantum computation robustness and adaptability.
